en: How can one tall tower split a barrel of black crude oil into gasoline, diesel and even road tar?
Take a guess.
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
Let's climb inside the tower.
Early on, oil was simply boiled in a big pot.
The vapor was cooled in a coiled pipe and dripped out as liquid.
Then the leftovers were drained and the pot refilled. Slow and messy.
Here's the secret.
Crude oil is a mix of many molecules. Some boil easily, others only when really hot.
So the crude is cleaned, then pumped through a furnace and heated to hundreds of degrees.
Part of it turns into vapor.
Inside the tower, the vapor rises while the liquid falls.
The tower is stacked with trays, covered in little metal bubble caps.
Rising vapor is forced under each cap and has to bubble through the liquid on the tray.
The bottom is hot and the top is cooler.
On every tray, heavier molecules cool and stay behind, while lighter ones keep climbing.
So each height collects a different product.
Gasoline at the top, kerosene and diesel in the middle, heavy oils near the bottom.
At the top, the vapor is cooled.
Some of that liquid is sent back down to wash the rising vapor, so the split gets cleaner.
The heaviest leftovers go to a second tower at low pressure, and the last sticky bits become road asphalt.
After all the refining, a forty two gallon barrel gives about nineteen to twenty gallons of gasoline in US refineries.
So one tall tower sorts crude oil by boiling point, floor by floor.
Stay curious!
